one_line_contribution: A clause-level causal test of the claim that an optimizer-evolved instruction and a retrieved memory item are informational substitutes rather than complements: deleting the one instruction clause a memory item duplicates should restore that item's marginal value while deleting a length-matched unrelated clause should not, with the accuracy-optimal memory-injection budget k* predicted to collapse as the instruction absorbs procedural content.
closest_prior_work: MemMachine (arXiv:2604.04853), which the authors themselves name: it already reports that prompt design and retrieval depth must be co-optimized and that prompt choice changes retrieval's marginal value across depths. That is the substitution *observation*, so E1's interaction test — the proposal's largest and best-powered experiment — is confirmatory of something already on record. The proposal concedes this and relocates its novelty entirely into E4 (clause knockout), which is by its own power analysis the weakest test in the plan (MDE ~4 points on a second difference). Secondarily, arXiv:2412.15266 ('On the Structural Memory of LLM Agents') already establishes flat/plateauing K-curves, which makes the 'high-k regime {4,8}' half of P1 empirically shaky before the grid is run; and MIPROv2 already formalizes prompt = instructions + demonstrations with a searched demonstration count, so the framing (not the interaction measurement) is not new. Redundancy gating itself is explicitly conceded to FILCO/RECOMP/MMR, correctly. Net: novelty is one experiment deep, and that experiment is the underpowered one.
strongest_objection: E4, the load-bearing mechanism test, contains an internal contradiction between its prediction (P2) and its own pre-registered confound gate. Substitution predicts m* gains marginal value under the targeted knockout B (= I3 minus clause c(m*)) because m* now supplies information the instruction no longer carries. But information can only be restored if it was worth something: if c(m*) contributes X accuracy points at k=0, then B0 is worse than A0 by ~X, and the recoverable DiD is bounded above by ~X. The gate demands that B0 and C0 be 'indistinguishable within the noise floor' — i.e. that X be smaller than the noise floor — which caps the true DiD *below the noise floor* and far below the stated MDE of ~4 points. So the two outcomes are: the gate passes and the DiD is guaranteed null by construction (reported as 'refuted' or 'underpowered'), or the DiD is large enough to detect and the gate almost certainly fails, at which point the authors have pre-committed to declaring it confounded. Either way E4 cannot confirm P2. The confound is not incidental: c(m*) is selected as the clause most duplicated by a retrieved item for *this query*, i.e. the most query-relevant clause, while c' is selected as a clause no retrieved item duplicates, i.e. the least query-relevant clause. B and C are matched on length but systematically anti-matched on relevance. A secondary version of the same objection: even if a positive DiD survives, it is equally well explained by 'memory can supply procedure the instruction is missing' — a far weaker and less interesting claim than instruction-conditioned redundancy — because nothing in the design distinguishes m* restoring *the specific duplicated content* from m* restoring *any* removed query-relevant procedure. Layered on top: the proposal's own pilot evidence (7 items harmed, 3 items did not, under a non-optimized instruction) already implies argmax-k is low under a minimal instruction, which contradicts P1's premise that argmax-k sits in {4,8} under I0 and would render the pre-registered 'regime shift' unobservable; and the E1 gate (I3 must beat I0 at k=0 beyond the noise floor) is likely to fire, since the track's own prior result is that prompt evolution fixed as many items as it broke and moved only the class-balanced metric.
what_would_fix_it: (1) Rebuild E4 as a dose-response rather than a binary knockout: pre-measure each clause's standalone k=0 contribution on a held-out split, then predict that the DiD scales with the measured clause effect. This replaces the self-defeating 'B0 must equal C0' gate with the correct control (regress item-recovery on clause-importance, and show recovery exceeds what a non-duplicating item recovers from the same clause deletion). (2) Match B and C on query-relevance, not just token length — the placebo clause must be one that is query-relevant but duplicated by no retrieved item, and its standalone effect must be matched to c(m*)'s; also replace deletion with neutral-filler substitution so instruction length is held constant. (3) Add the arm that actually isolates relational redundancy: under the targeted knockout B, inject a *non-duplicating* item of matched retrieval score. Substitution requires m* to recover more than that item does; 'memory fills any instruction gap' predicts they recover equally. (4) Add the missing instruction-side length placebo (below). (5) Drop argmax-k as a pre-registered confirmatory statistic — it is an argmax over five noisy point estimates with no stated inferential procedure and no CI; fit k* from the interaction model with a bootstrap CI instead. (6) Execute the collision search before submission rather than committing to it, and reduce the primary grid (E1 duplicates MemMachine's observation) to fund the mechanism arms above.
missing_baseline: An instruction-side length/content placebo: I0 plus length-matched, topically plausible but procedurally empty instruction text, matched to I3-s1's token count, evaluated across the same k grid. As written, every step of the ladder (I0 -> I1 -> I3, and I_H, which is a *strong* instruction and so cannot serve as neutral filler) confounds procedural content with instruction length, and longer instructions change where memory items sit in the context window and how much attention budget they get. E2 pads only the *memory* slot, so the entire lost-in-the-middle / prompt-length explanation of the negative interaction is untested on the axis where it actually operates. A reviewer would also demand a random-bank control — real memory items sampled off-query at matched k — to separate 'any injected item costs interference' from 'instruction-duplicating items cost interference'; E2's synthetic padding is not a substitute for real-but-non-duplicating retrieved text.
preprint_collision: Weak, and the proposal says so itself: the search tool failed on every attempt and *zero queries were executed this round*, so the submission contains no executed novelty search. Per the standard that an unsearched claim of novelty is a weakness rather than a neutral, this alone justifies a markdown. The carried-forward evidence is a five-query capped search flagged as provisional, and the authors explicitly write that if MemMachine or a successor already contains a clause-level or item-level causal test, 'this proposal collides and should not be run in its current form' — that is an unresolved, self-identified collision risk in the fastest-moving corner of this literature (2026 context-curation, memory-budget, and instruction-retrieval-interaction preprints appear monthly). I was not able to verify the cited identifiers independently, and most are given as bare arXiv numbers (2604.27003, 2604.27283, 2603.02473, 2604.24334) without titles or authors, which makes them uncheckable as written and would draw a request for full citations. Credit where due: the honesty is exemplary and the commitment to a >=15-query search plus a partial-collision fallback design is the right response — but a commitment to search is not a search, and the novelty score reflects an unestablished, not a disproven, novelty claim.
